title: The river cut off
hookLine: at Karbala his camp is surrounded and cut off from the Euphrates

cards: Somewhere on the road to Kufa, the histories say, a troop of horsemen rides up to block Husayn's way. Their commander is al-Hurr. The men have been riding in the heat, and they are parched, and so are their horses.

Husayn tells his young men to give them water, and the horses too. The reports say they filled bowls and held them to the horses' mouths, again and again, until each had drunk. These were the soldiers sent to stop him.
A few days later, on a plain by the Euphrates called Karbala, the water would run the other way.

teach.b: Kufa does not welcome him. Muslim ibn Aqil, the cousin he sent ahead, has been caught and killed, and the city that wrote all those letters has gone quiet under its new governor, Ubaydullah ibn Ziyad.
Husayn is turned aside, and his small camp pitches its tents at Karbala, in the open, near the river.
Then a much larger army arrives, and the histories report an order from the governor: put yourselves between Husayn and the water; do not let them taste a drop. So soldiers line the riverbank.
The Euphrates is close enough to see, and the camp, with its children, its women and its old men, cannot reach it.
The reports say Husayn's half-brother al-Abbas led a party down to the river by night and fought his way back with some water skins.
Shia Muslims remember al-Abbas with deep love as the one who carried water, and the stories of his last attempt are told with great tenderness in Muharram.
The same camp that had watered its enemies' horses on the road is now refused water by men who have more than enough.
The Qur'an says that God made every living thing from water; to cut a family off from a river is to cut at life itself.

That is one reason water carries this story in Shia remembrance: a glass offered to a stranger during Muharram can be a memory of Karbala. And it is why the plainest line of this story is also the hardest.

how: In Muharram, Shia Muslims remember the thirst of Husayn's camp at Karbala, and some communities set up stalls to offer water and drinks to passersby in memory of it.

practice: If you can, pour a glass of water and hold it, noticing how easy it was to get. Bring to mind the camp at Karbala, near enough to see the river and unable to reach it, then drink slowly, a sip at a time.
If you pray, you can say bismillah before you drink and alhamdulillah after; if not, just notice each sip.

wordCard.voice: Karbala. The plain by the Euphrates where Husayn's camp was cut off from the river, and soldiers stood between a family and the water. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: thirst, a word heard often in the elegies of Karbala.

carryVoice: Your line: they were thirsty. A glass of water can carry their memory. That's day eight hundred ninety.

Qur'an 21:30 (God made every living thing from water)
